questions.q: What problem does the Selector pattern specifically solve?
options: It centralizes all SOQL for a given object into one class, so the same query isn't duplicated and drifting across multiple classes
It prevents governor limit breaches automatically
It replaces the need for triggers entirely
It encrypts sensitive fields before querying them
questions.explain: A Selector class centralizes an object's queries in one place, so every caller gets consistent results and a query change only needs to happen in one spot.

questions.q: What is a Service class responsible for, as distinct from a Selector class?
options: Running scheduled jobs only
Storing custom metadata type records
Holding the actual business logic — the rules about what should happen — separate from data access and from the triggering event
Exposing a REST endpoint
questions.explain: A Service class owns the business rule itself, while the Selector owns fetching the data and the trigger handler owns detecting the event — each layer has a distinct, separate responsibility.

questions.q: Is the Selector/Service layering pattern enforced by the Salesforce platform itself?
options: Yes, Apex will not compile a trigger that embeds SOQL directly
Yes, but only for Enterprise Edition orgs
No, and it was deprecated by Salesforce in a recent release
No — it's a widely-used community convention, strongly associated with open-source frameworks like Apex Enterprise Patterns (fflib), not a platform-mandated structure
questions.explain: Nothing in Salesforce requires this structure — it's a community convention for organizing larger codebases, popularized in part by open-source frameworks, not something the platform enforces.

questions.q: In the layered example, what does the trigger handler's role shrink to once Selector and Service classes are introduced?
options: Writing the SOQL query itself, since Selectors can't be called from triggers
Detecting the event and dispatching to the appropriate Service method
Nothing — the trigger handler becomes unnecessary and is deleted
Handling all governor-limit checks directly
questions.explain: With Selector and Service classes in place, the trigger handler's job narrows to detecting the event (which context, which records) and delegating to the Service method that implements the actual rule.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when might introducing a full Selector/Service layer NOT be worth it?
options: For a small org with a simple trigger where the extra classes add more structure than the actual complexity warrants
Never — it should always be used for every object regardless of complexity
Only when the org has more than one million records
Only in sandboxes, never in production
questions.explain: For simple cases, a handful of extra classes can be more overhead than the complexity justifies — the pattern earns its cost once multiple pieces of automation genuinely need to share the same data or logic.
